title: Contracts & Instruments
hook: MNQ isn't just a ticker on your screen. Know what you're actually trading.

launchpad.outcome: Name the common futures instruments and explain the difference between a mini and a micro contract.
launchpad.missionQuestion: If someone switches from 1 MNQ contract to 1 NQ contract, does their risk stay the same?

slides.body: A futures contract is a standardized agreement tied to an underlying asset or benchmark, under specs set by the exchange. When you trade futures, you're trading contracts whose values move with their underlying market — not buying shares of a company.

check.prompt: A trader moves from MNQ to NQ but keeps the same number of contracts because "the chart looks the same."

options.label: That's a mistake
options.body: The contract multiplier is different, so the same price move produces very different P&L and risk.
options.why: Exactly — the chart shape being similar doesn't mean the dollar exposure is similar.

options.label: That's fine
options.body: NQ and MNQ are the same size, just different tickers.
options.feedback: They're not the same size — MNQ is 1/10 the contract multiplier of NQ.

slides.title: Micro vs. mini — same market, different size

items.label: Always verify
items.desc: Contract specs differ — check the exchange.

slides.quote: Never choose your number of contracts because someone else trades that size. Know the instrument. Know its value. Know your risk.

slides.body: Same underlying market, different contract multiplier — always check the specs before you trade.

check.prompt: Which pair correctly matches the instrument to its name?

options.label: MGC → Micro Gold
options.why: MGC is Micro Gold. ES is the full-size E-mini S&P 500 (MES is the micro), and MNQ is the micro version of NQ.

options.label: ES → Micro E-mini S&P 500
options.feedback: ES is the full-size E-mini S&P 500 — MES is the micro version.

options.label: MNQ → E-mini Nasdaq-100
options.feedback: MNQ is the MICRO E-mini Nasdaq-100 — NQ is the full-size version.

slides.body: Contract count changes your exposure — never the instrument itself.

check.prompt: A trader switches from trading 1 contract of MNQ to 5 contracts of MNQ. Has she changed instruments?

options.label: No
options.body: She's still trading MNQ; only her size and dollar exposure changed.
options.why: The instrument stays MNQ — contract count only changes exposure.

options.label: Yes
options.body: 5 contracts makes it a different instrument.
options.feedback: Contract count never changes what instrument you're trading.

slides.prompt: Imagine another AGHF girl asks: "What's actually different between MNQ and NQ?" How would you explain it to her?
slides.modelAnswer: They're the same underlying market — the Nasdaq-100 — just different contract sizes. MNQ is the micro version, worth 1/10 of what NQ is per point. So the exact same price move means very different dollar risk depending on which one you're trading.

takeaways: A futures contract's value moves with its underlying market — it isn't ownership.
Micro contracts (MNQ, MES, MGC) are a fraction of their mini counterparts (NQ, ES, GC).
Contract count changes your exposure, not the instrument itself.
remember: Know the instrument. Know its value. Know your risk.
